title: Spill the T+1: How AI, BNPL, and Marketplace Fatigue Are Reshaping E-Commerce in Southeast Asia
summary: Southeast Asia's e-commerce is growing fast again. Learn how AI shopping, BNPL, and rising marketplace costs are changing how brands sell online. The post Spill the T+1: How AI, BNPL, and Marketplace Fatigue Are Reshaping E-Commerce in Southeast Asia appeared first on Xendit .
body_markdown:
E-commerce in Southeast Asia is speeding up again, but the cost of selling on marketplaces keeps rising, and shoppers are changing how they discover and pay for products. In this episode of


*Spill the T+1* ,


**Ina Gatan** , Head of GTM Philippines, and


**Simon Torring** , Co-Founder of Cube Asia, combine on-the-ground merchant insights with regional e-commerce data to explain what's driving the shift, and what brands need to get right as they look beyond the marketplace.


They cover:


- Why e-commerce growth in Southeast Asia is re-accelerating after years of steady growth, led by platforms like Shopee and TikTok Shop.


- How BNPL is becoming a hidden growth engine, from large-ticket purchases moving online to BNPL providers in the Philippines accepting QR Ph payments.


- Why rising commissions and advertising fees are pushing brands to consider their own brand.com, and why leaving marketplaces isn't as simple as it sounds.


- How generative AI is changing where the shopping journey starts, and what that means for where consumers end up buying.


- Why electronics is among the first categories to feel the squeeze, and why shoppers will pay more for trust and peace of mind.


## **The Second Growth Spurt**


**Simon** : I mean, e-commerce is like a roller coaster. For the last couple of years, we've been settled in a sort of even pattern around 13 to 15% annual growth. But then what we've seen in the last two or three quarters is actually a meaningful re-acceleration.


**Ina:** Despite the lower growth rate?


**Simon:** Exactly. So it's kind of sped up again. And especially when we look at some of the big e-commerce platforms like Shopee and TikTok Shop, they're growing faster than we thought would be possible in this stage of the market growth.


## **Meeting Consumers Where They Are**


**Ina:** When I think about it, right? I mean, like, not just in the e-commerce space. At the end of the day, we just want our lives to be easier, right? Like, as a consumer. So whatever part of the process, of the buying process you're in, you just want to make it super, super easy. That's why, like, when we talk to different merchants and different clients at Xendit, when people talk about conversion, they don't just want to look at the metric from when the time that they input the payment until it goes through. They're thinking about, you know, the journey. Is it easy for me to locate the product? Am I able to compare actually between certain products? Which one is better for me? And then when I get to the payments, like, if this is something that I actually use and then I come back, do I need to input my payment details again? A lot of that is really, really important.


## **BNPL as a Hidden Growth Engine**


**Ina:** You said earlier something about BNPL. Where do you see BNPL, like, becoming a big driver for the group?


**Simon:** Yeah. So I think buy now, pay later (BNPL) has been a, it's one of the modes of payment in e-commerce that we have seen consistently growing as a share total over the last couple of years. And I think especially what we've noticed recently is that some of the big e-commerce platforms are now integrating it directly into their platform. I think that's making it very easy for consumers to use. Therefore, adoption goes up.


But we also have this theory that buy now, pay later and this access to consumer credit is also one of the things that's making e-commerce grow faster. We believe that, especially for some large-ticket items like electronics, motorbikes, and things like that, consumers are actually starting to maybe browse offline, but end up making the purchase online because they can get access to credit easier than they can offline.


So again, it's a working theory, but we have really been puzzled by, like, "Wow, how can e-commerce be growing so fast at the moment?" So we're looking for these new, like, clues and ideas about what could be causing this.


**Ina:** Yeah, that's super interesting, because when I look at the BNPL space in the Philippines, all of these BNPL providers who have, like, millions and millions and millions of users already, and borrowers, they themselves enable what we call QR Ph, which is our national QR, like, payment rail. So you can actually scan a QR Ph code using any BNPL channel.


I was meeting with a fast-food provider, basically. And this fast-food provider, there's a part of their business where they have to accept large-ticket items. This person was like, "You know, I need you to aggregate all of the buy now, pay later channels for me." The ticket size was big. He wants to make it accessible, everything that you just said.


And as you were speaking earlier, I was thinking about why is a marketplace, like, why is BNPL such a big driver? It's because, like you said, the marketplaces are the ones that are enabling it. So the users are actually there. So there's still a way for end users to actually, for brands to reach, you know, the users of BNPL providers, not being maybe on a marketplace or not being associated with this, but still capturing that.


## **Marketplace Fatigue: Why Brands Want Out**


**Simon:** Yeah. I mean, look, I think what's happening is, we work with a lot of heads of e-commerce. I think nowadays, almost all heads of e-commerce are kind of fantasizing about having their own brand.com, because the rent, so to speak, on the marketplaces is going up. The commission rates are going up. Mandatory advertising fees are going up. So it's getting more and more expensive for them to sell.


So I think everybody's dreaming of that moment where they can say, "You know, I can save some cost, but also I can own more of the customer data. I can own more of the customer experience," right? But I think that the inconvenient truth for now is that a lot of the innovations of e-commerce payments at least starts right now on the big e-commerce platforms.


So I think when heads of e-commerce are having these deliberations, there's also going to be a need for them to think about: is there a consumer experience gap between my marketplace presence and my brand.com presence, right? To audit that and to benchmark that, because the consumers in the end will just go where it's easiest to buy.


**Ina:** Exactly, exactly. Which brings us back to, I remember the other day we were talking about what is Cube's, or yours, or Cube Asia's hypothesis for the next two years. And I would love for you to say it again for the people who are listening here.


**Simon:** Yeah, I think so. There's a couple of interesting things going on. So one, the re-acceleration of e-commerce, I think, is exciting for everybody who's selling online. The second is, as the costs of selling online have gone up, I think we're now getting into the realm where it might be more palatable for e-commerce companies to start selling on their own brand, brand.com, or through e-retail and things like that. So maybe the tipping point back to a deconsolidation, where we will see less marketplace concentration, maybe that's coming closer.


Could I get now my opportunity to get a bit more freedom and independence from these marketplaces who have made my P&L harder and harder in the last few years? Then, looking a little bit further ahead, I think this is also such an exciting time because of the rise of generative AI and consumer use of AI tools. More than half of online shoppers in Southeast Asia are now using these GenAI tools in their shopping process.


The norm would be a consumer who, instead of going on Google and searching for a product category or going on Shopee and searching for a product category, they're now actually starting the journey on ChatGPT or Gemini or something like that, saying perhaps, "You know, I'm looking for an electric toothbrush. You know, I'm traveling a lot. What if I can't carry the charger around? You know, what should I look for?" And then, you know, you'd get some product recommendations.


**Ina:** Like, I go and tell ChatGPT, like, "Okay, my hair has been really weird recently. This is a photo. Like, you know, can you, like, what's the best type? Like, do I look for sulfate-free with a brand that's in the Philippines that I can buy? Whatever, whatever." And the reason why I have those keywords is so important to me, because if it's not smart enough, it'll give me something from another country, and then I won't have the payment method that I need, and it's not going to be. So that's super, super cool.


## **Electronics: The Category Under Pressure**


**Ina:** I touched on it a little bit earlier on what this second, you know, this growth spurt really means. So today, we're seeing that, you know, most of the brands and the growth is actually driven from marketplaces. And you also mentioned it earlier that, you know, there's already, there's curiosity coming from certain brands.


Well, I guess my first question also is that, are there certain categories where you see that they're deciding, "Wait, this is not working for us. Should we start investing in a D2C?" So are there certain categories? And what types of questions are they asking when they actually make this decision to move to brand.com?


**Simon:** Yeah, I mean, I think that different forces at play, because you have, among all of the brands, there's kind of a scale of digital e-commerce maturity. And many of the brands are still quite early in that journey. And I think for most of them, they start on the big marketplaces. And that's probably what they ought to be doing, because it's easier and cheaper ways to get started. So I think they have a ways to go.


On the other hand, there's also a cut when we look at all of these brands, which is just, what do their unit economics look like? And what we can see, for example, in the last year or so, is that you have categories that are much more under pressure from the rising selling costs of e-commerce marketplaces. And it tends to be those that have quite low gross margins.


So, for example, electronics is a category where there's notoriously quite slim gross margins. And in that category, we have started to see in our data, for example, we see merchants that are decreasing in e-commerce sales year on year, which, at this stage of the growth journey, is almost weird, right?


**Ina:** The listings are being removed.


**Simon:** Listings are being removed, or just they're selling less. Maybe they're able to invest only a limited amount in subsidies and promos, so their products don't really show up on the e-commerce platform. So I think there are some categories where there's just, where the pressures of rising costs seem to be felt much sooner than in others.


**Ina:** You know, that actually, that makes sense, because electronics, it's also, like, not as straightforward as of a buying journey that you would think, right? Like, you know, it's very technical. You're going to want to check the spec. Like, having an agentic commerce-type tool attached to that buying process would actually essentially work also. And it's not something that you would actually buy impulsively. Maybe, is it? I'm not sure. Correct me if I'm wrong.


But I'm also thinking that electronics, at the end of the day, it's considered a more, like, premium product. And I think that you published a study, Cube Asia published a study, not sure how long ago, but that end users are actually willing to spend more for an experience that's more premium or more secure, right? And then maybe you can, can you maybe share a little bit about that?


## **Peace of Mind: What Consumers Will Pay For**


**Simon:** Absolutely. So, so look, I think, indeed, you know, online purchases fall on some spectrum between being very impulsive and then having a very long consideration path. And I think for a category like electronics, it will tend to fall on the higher and longer consideration cycle. I think that's then also affecting, like, what kind of purchase experience you want to have for that.


So yeah, some of the things we're seeing in the data is, for higher-ticket items, for branded items in particular, consumers are willing to pay a little bit more if they're buying it from a place where they feel a high degree of trust and safety. And I think that can either be the mall part of a platform like Lazada or Shopee, or it can be a brand.com where you know, "Okay, I'm buying it from the brand, or I'm buying it from an official distributor." Maybe I'll pay 3 or 5% more, but it's peace of mind, like the cost of peace of mind. At least what the data is showing is consumers are willing to make that trade-off.


But I think electronics is also a category that is particularly interesting for this GenAI purchase journey, because, as you mentioned, you know, this is a category where consumers would often, like, the old-school consumer journey is you go to a specialist store, right? And you want to talk to somebody. And I think that's the part of the purchase journey that GenAI is kind of augmenting or potentially replacing.


But therefore, I think the implications follow. Where are you then going to buy it from? You know, if your journey is starting there, do you then necessarily want to buy it from Shopee? Do you want to buy it from the brand.com? I think in the end, it comes down to price and the trust you feel in the place you're buying it, and then also just the convenience of how easy it is to buy.


**Ina:** Exactly. So, and these people are, they're already, I love what you said about peace of mind. Like, that's actually so important on the end-user side, and also on the brand side, on the merchant side. Like, "I'm investing so much into this, into my brand.com. I'm having it designed beautifully. I'm making sure the checkout process is great. But am I really making it accessible enough to the people that I want to reach it to?"


So I think one of the things that we do well at Xendit is that, you know, we try to really understand, you know, when you're talking about a category like electronics, who are the end users? What are they paying with usually on a day-to-day? So, because we don't want to, like, break the process, right? You have to meet your end users where they are.


And I think that's actually what's happening with all of these changes at the end of the day, right? The end users evolve and you meet them where they are. You can challenge them or you educate them in some way. But at the end of the day, again, it's all about making it easier for them. And how to keep up in this new wave is just to think about: make it easy.


**Simon:** Absolutely. Yeah. I think easier and cheaper and faster and better. No consumers are ever going to be bothered. Right. Awesome.
